summary: This work establishes a general framework for applying linear quantum error mitigation (QEM) techniques, including probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), zero-noise extrapolation, and symmetry verification, directly to physical qubits within quantum error correction (QEC) codes without modifying the QEC decoder. Using PEC on memory experiments, the authors analytically prove and numerically verify that the leading-order logical error probability is suppressed from $\mathcal{O}(p^{\lceil d/2 \rceil})$ to $\mathcal{O}(p^{\lceil d/2 \rceil + 1})$, effectively increasing the code distance by 2.
motivation: Early fault-tolerant quantum computers face stringent qubit budgets and modest code distances where neither QEC nor QEM alone suffices; a hybrid strategy combining both is essential to maximize computational power.
method: The framework exploits the linearity of QEC to show that any linear QEM method can be composed with QEC as $\mathbb{E}[\hat{O}_{\mathrm{emc}}] = \langle\langle O | \mathcal{R} | \rho_{\mathrm{em}} \rangle\rangle$ without requiring decoder modification. For PEC, an approximate inversion process $\mathcal{F} = \frac{1}{A}(P_0 \mathcal{I} - P_\omega \sum_{|K|=\omega} \mathcal{G}_K)$ targets weight-$\omega = \lceil d/2 \rceil$ errors before applying QEC with a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder.
result: For distance-3 repetition codes and surface codes, PEC achieves logical error rates comparable to distance-5 unmitigated codes while using 40% and 64% fewer qubits, respectively; however, the error threshold decreases to $p_{\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{PEC}} \approx 0.19$ (repetition) and $0.03$ (surface) from $p_{\mathrm{th}} \approx 0.32$ and $0.12$ unmitigated.
